stories.title: Japan to extend weather forecasts in response to climate change
stories.summary: Japan's Meteorological Agency plans to extend weather forecasts from seven days to two weeks by 2030 to better prepare for extreme weather events. Climate change is increasing the frequency and severity of dangerous weather in Japan, including record heat and deadly rains. Longer forecasts will help with early preparations, such as securing manpower for snow removal, improving safety and response measures. Japan’s meteorological agency said on Aug 26 it plans to start issuing two-week forecasts to better prepare for extreme weather events, up from seven days at present. Like elsewhere, human-induced climate change is increasing the frequency and intensity of dangerous weather in Japan, scientists say. In 2025, the country had its hottest summer on record and earlier in August torrential rains in the Chiba region killed at least 13 people. Currently the Japan Meteorological Agency (JMA) issues forecasts for the following seven days. But an expert report commissioned by the JMA said that advances in climate data observations and simulations made it possible – and desirable – to extend this to two weeks. “Extended period of weather forecasts with warnings will help better preparations for extreme weather that have been frequently observed in recent years, something which is driven by global warming,” JMA official Masayuki Kyoda told AFP. “We have heard, for example, that it takes two weeks to secure manpower needed for snow removal. You can’t gather people quickly to clear snow,” added Kyoda, who is in charge of analysing abnormal weather for the agency.

stories.title: At least 14 newborns killed in Pakistan hospital nursery fire
stories.summary: Only one child rescued after fire breaks out in nursery at Pakistan Institute of Medical Sciences Hospital, Geo News reports. At least 14 newborn babies have been killed after a fire broke out in the nursery of a government-run hospital in Pakistan’s capital, Islamabad, according to officials. The blaze started shortly before 07:00am local time (02:00 GMT) on Wednesday on the third floor of the Mother and Child Centre at the Pakistan Institute of Medical Sciences (PIMS) Hospital. Local broadcaster Geo TV put the death toll at 15, and said one infant was rescued from the ward before firefighters managed to extinguish the flames. In a statement posted on social media platform X, Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif offered his condolences to the bereaved families and ordered an immediate investigation into the incident. He promised that those responsible would face the “strictest action”. Initial reports from officials indicate the fire was likely caused by a short circuit in a malfunctioning air conditioning unit. Building fires are a frequent occurrence in Pakistan, where safety regulations and building codes are routinely ignored or poorly enforced. In January, at least 65 people died when a massive fire swept through a crowded shopping complex in the southern port city of Karachi. Wednesday’s blaze is one of the deadliest hospital fires in Pakistan’s history. While the government provides subsidised medical treatment through public hospitals, the state sector remains severely underfunded, mismanaged, and overcrowded.
